title: Mr. G’s Pizzeria marks 30 years as friendship preserves legacy | Bryan - College Station - Community Impact
content: As Mr. G’s Pizzeria celebrates three decades in downtown Bryan, owner Susan Carnes reflects on the unlikely friendship preserving the restaurant’s legacy and inspiring its next chapter. For years, customers walking into Mr. G’s Pizzeria in Historic Downtown Bryan were likely to find founder Giovanni “Mr. G” Cerone sitting at a dining room table, paperwork spread out before him as he greeted regulars, welcomed newcomers and shared stories from a life that had taken him from Italy to Texas. Nearly five years after Mr. G's passing, that presence still lingers inside the 30-year-old restaurant. His recipes remain, as do many of the traditions which made the pizzeria a downtown Bryan institution. Now, as the restaurant celebrates its 30th anniversary, the family he chose is carrying his legacy into the business’s next chapter. Mr. G’s Pizzeria will celebrate 30 years in business this month while expanding its footprint with the opening of g’s Southside Italian Cafe in College Station. The new café, expected to open with a soft launch in mid-July before a grand opening this fall, isn’t replacing the downtown restaurant. Instead, owner Susan Carnes described it as “a nod and a tribute” to Mr. G. Carnes wasn’t looking to own a restaurant when she first met Mr. G. She and her husband had just celebrated their 10-year anniversary at Downtown Uncorked, which was located in downtown Bryan until it moved to south College Station in 2021. The couple stopped into Mr. G’s to grab a pizza for their children at home. Instead, Carnes found herself talking with the restaurant’s owner for nearly two hours. “It was like love at first sight, friendship at first sight,” she said with a laugh. “These two families just adopted each other.” “He says–in his little Italian accent–he goes, ‘Susan, if you [don’t] take it, [I’ll] close at the end of the month,’” she recalled him saying. Although she had little restaurant experience beyond waiting tables in college, Carnes and her family stepped in during the uncertainty of the COVID-19 pandemic. Today, her children have grown up inside the business much like several employees who have spent decades there. One longtime pizza cook has worked at Mr. G’s since she was 15 years old, and Carnes’ teenage son will soon bus tables at the new café. Mr. G’s widow Houda remains closely involved and has even shared recipes from her former College Station restaurant, Cenare, for the new concept. Much has changed since Mr. G’s opened in 1996, but the recipes that built its reputation remain largely untouched. The restaurant continues to serve its signature pizzas from classic Margherita and Hawaiian pies to house specialties like the Lu Pizza, which is topped with mozzarella, feta, caramelized onions and prosciutto. The menu also includes calzones, pasta, subs, salads, garlic bread, gluten-free and keto options and desserts like tiramisu and cannoli. At the heart of it all is the pizza dough recipe Mr. G. brought to Bryan decades ago. Today, Carnes said only two people know how to make it. While the downtown pizzeria will continue serving its signature and longtime favorites, the new café will expand on the family’s Italian roots. The kitchen at the College Station location will also become the primary location for preparing dough, sauces and other ingredients used by both restaurants. Despite the expansion, Carnes said Bryan remains home. She calls the downtown restaurant a “7,000 square-foot elephant” that has survived recessions, COVID-19 and decades of changing restaurant trends. “It would leave a hole in the heart,” she said. “So, as long as we’re able, Mr. G’s downtown Bryan will be [here].” The restaurant continues to draw crowds during First Friday events, hosts live entertainment and private events and remains one of downtown Bryan’s long-running eateries. For Carnes, opening another restaurant isn’t about growing a brand nearly as much as preserving a friendship. The lowercase “g” in g’s Southside Italian Cafe was intentional, she said, as it’s not meant to replace or compete with Mr. G’s. Carnes told Community Impact Mr G’s plans to have specials and parties to celebrate 30 years. In the meantime, Mr. G’s will operate during normal business hours, staying open until 9 p.m. during the week and 10 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. title: GS Group Builds Asia's Largest AI Data Center in Donghae - 조선일보
content: 120-trillion-won project in Donghae to reach 2.4GW by 2029, positioning Gangwon as AI hub GS Group is building Asia’s largest AI data center in Donghae, Gangwon Province. It is a mega-project with a maximum investment of 120 trillion Korean won, to be developed to a scale of 2.4GW by 2029. Amid a global surge in demand for data centers due to AI expansion, Gangwon Province has moved to establish itself as a hub for AI infrastructure. Gangwon Province, Donghae City, and GS Group signed a business agreement on the 6th at a small meeting room in the Gangwon Provincial Government Office to establish the ‘Donghae AI Data Center Campus.’ Those attending the agreement ceremony included Gangwon Governor Woo Sang-ho, Donghae Mayor Lee Jeong-hak, GS Vice Chairman Hong Soon-gi, and GS E&R Representative Hwang Byeong-so. The Donghae AI Data Center will be built on approximately 70,000 pyeong of land within the Bukpyeong Second General Industrial Complex in Donghae City. The plan is to first construct 1.2GW by 2028, then add another 1.2GW by 2029 to complete a total scale of 2.4GW. As a single AI data center, it will be the largest in Asia. GS announced the plan to build the Donghae AI Data Center at the ‘National Report Meeting on the Three Mega Projects for Korea’s Great Leap Forward’ on the 29th of last month. The total investment cost is 30 trillion Korean won, and including costs for graphics processing units (GPUs) and memory, it is expected to reach up to 120 trillion Korean won. The project site, the Bukpyeong Second General Industrial Complex, is an industrial complex that GS began construction on in 2016 and completed in 2022. With the site already secured and power supply conditions in place, the project is expected to proceed swiftly. Measures to secure power and water, the core elements of an AI data center, have also been prepared. The 1.2GW-scale facility to be built by 2028 will receive power linked to GS Donghae Power’s power generation facilities. The cooling system will operate using an immersion cooling method, where servers are submerged in special cooling oil, and approximately 1,100 tons of industrial water per day. Gangwon Province plans to operate a fast-track system for permits and licenses to allow companies to focus on investment, and actively support infrastructure such as power and water supply. Governor Woo’s first official order upon taking office on the 1st to form the ‘AI Data Center Promotion Team’ was also aimed at accelerating the project. This agreement is significant as it marks the realization of Governor Woo’s vision for fostering the AI industry, which he revealed in an interview with this newspaper last week. At the time, Governor Woo disclosed that alongside GS’s 2.4GW project in Donghae, SK Group is also pushing to build a 1GW-scale AI data center in the Gangwon region. If SK’s project proceeds, Gangwon Province could become the country’s largest AI infrastructure cluster with a total of 3.4GW-scale AI data centers. Globally, competition to secure AI data centers is intensifying. McKinsey & Company, a global consulting firm, projected that while demand for AI data centers will grow by 19–22% annually, supply will lag, leading to a shortage of approximately 15GW in the U.S. alone by 2030. Consequently, global companies are expanding AI infrastructure investments to regions outside the U.S. Gangwon Province highlights its strengths: abundant power supply, vast industrial land, and relatively fewer location restrictions. AI data centers are power-intensive industries that consume far more electricity than general data centers, giving regions capable of large-scale power supply a competitive edge. The capital region faces difficulties in adding large-scale AI data centers due to saturated power grids. Gangwon Governor Woo Sang-ho stated, “AI data centers are the core infrastructure of the AI industry and the growth foundation that will determine future industrial competitiveness. The Donghae AI Data Center will be the starting point for building Gangwon’s AI industry ecosystem and a key hub for enhancing South Korea’s AI industry competitiveness.”

title: South Korean prosecutors indict four major refiners over allegations of oil price collusion - CNBC
content:
South Korean prosecutors on Monday indicted four major domestic oil refiners for violating fair trade laws, alleging they colluded to drive up domestic fuel prices following the Middle East conflict. HD Hyundai Oilbank, SK Energy, GS Caltex, and S-Oil were the four companies that breached the nation’s fair trade act, according to Yonhap News Agency. HD Hyundai Oilbank and SK Energy colluded on 14.2 trillion won ($9.2 billion) worth of oil sales, Yonhap reported, citing prosecutors. Factoring in GS Caltex and S-Oil, which allegedly mimicked those prices, the total anticompetitive impact stands at roughly 26 trillion won, the report said. The investigation was initiated after domestic oil prices sharply rose following the U.S.–Iran conflict, prosecutors said, finding that collusion by pricing executives at two of the firms over the timing and scale of the hikes was the primary driver. The prosecution said the collusion was not a standalone incident but a long-standing, systemic practice that surfaced during a time of global crisis. In March, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung warned on X that oil refiners and corporations engaged in price-fixing would be held accountable, vowing to deploy all lawful measures against unethical business practices. Shares of the oil refiners and their owners were still higher. S-Oil gained 6.08%, SK Innovation, a parent company for SK Energy, advanced 1.58% while HD Hyundai rose 1.21% and GS Holdings, which jointly controls refiner GS Caltex with Chevron through its energy unit, rose 6.99%. S-Oil declined to comment. Hyundai Oilbank, SK Energy, GS Caltex could not be immediately reached for comment. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. title: GS Group to Build 2.4GW AI Data Center Campus in Donghae, Signs MOU with Gangwon Province - finance.biggo.com
content: GS Group will develop a total 2.4GW (gigawatt) artificial intelligence (AI) data center campus in Donghae City, Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. Gangwon Province plans to use this project as the starting point for the region's AI industry ecosystem and is committed to providing full support for corporate investment and administrative assistance. Gangwon Province announced on the morning of July 6 that it had signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Donghae City and GS Group for the development of the "Donghae AI Data Center." The signing ceremony was attended by key officials including Woo Sang-ho, Governor of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province; Lee Jeong-hak, Mayor of Donghae City; Hong Soon-ki, Vice Chairman of GS; Hwang Byung-so, CEO of GS E&R; Do Hyun-soo, CEO of GS AI Infrastructure; and Lee Cheol-hyu, Head of KEPCO's Gangwon Headquarters. The agreement was pursued in line with the South Korean government's policy to strengthen AI industry competitiveness and promote balanced regional development. The core focus is to build an AI data center campus on approximately 231,000 square meters of land within Donghae's Bukpyeong Second General Industrial Complex, foster the AI infrastructure industry around it, and revitalize the local economy. Under the agreement, Gangwon Province, Donghae City, and GS will cooperate on: attracting companies and fostering the AI infrastructure industry for the successful development of the Donghae AI Data Center Campus; providing swift administrative support including a permitting fast track; and establishing and operating a working-level consultative body for ongoing coordination. The Donghae AI Data Center Campus will be built in phases. The goal is to first develop 1.2GW of capacity by 2028, then expand by an additional 1.2GW by 2029, completing a large-scale AI infrastructure totaling 2.4GW. The project will leverage GS's existing power generation infrastructure and the locational advantages of the Bukpyeong Second General Industrial Complex. "AI data centers are the core infrastructure of the AI industry and the growth foundation driving future industrial competitiveness," said Gangwon Governor Woo Sang-ho at the signing ceremony. "The Donghae AI Data Center Campus will be Gangwon's first AI industry project and the starting point for building an AI industry ecosystem." Governor Woo expressed strong determination regarding the speed of administrative processing, which companies consider critically important. "With the mindset that companies focus on investment while the province takes responsibility for administration, we will actively support them at the speed they desire," he said, promising GS Group "administrative support at a speed that will surprise you." He added, "Let us work together so that Gangwon's talent can grow while working at major corporations." Positive prospects also emerged regarding power supply, a critical factor for AI data center operations. Lee Cheol-hyu, Head of KEPCO's Gangwon Headquarters, stated, "Until now, Gangwon Province, despite having abundant energy resources, had to send surplus power to the Seoul metropolitan area and South Korea's Chungcheong region due to limited local industry. But now that large-scale investments by major companies are materializing, we will actively support all power-related aspects." title: GS Group Breaks Ground on $19.6 Billion AI Data Center in Donghae, Aiming for Asia's Largest by 2028 - finance.biggo.com
content: GS Group is moving full speed ahead with the construction of a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center in Donghae, Gangwon State, with a direct investment of approximately 30 trillion won (approximately $19.6 billion). The total project cost, including GPUs and memory, is estimated to reach 120 trillion won (approximately $78.4 billion), and upon completion, the facility is expected to be the largest in Asia. Gangwon State, Donghae City, and GS signed a business agreement for the development of the "Donghae AI Data Center" at the provincial government's conference room on July 6. The signing ceremony was attended by Gangwon Governor Woo Sang-ho, Donghae Mayor Lee Jeong-hak, GS Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki, GS E&R CEO Hwang Byung-so, GS AI Infrastructure CEO Do Hyun-soo, and Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) Gangwon Headquarters Chief Lee Cheol-hyu, among others. The core of this agreement lies in maximizing the speed of project execution through administrative support, including a fast-track permitting and approval process and infrastructure development. The three parties agreed to jointly address key issues arising during the project and to form a working-level consultative body to facilitate smooth progress. The Donghae AI Data Center campus will be built on an approximately 70,000-pyeong site within the Bukpyeong 2nd General Industrial Complex. The plan targets initial completion of 1.2GW capacity by December 2028, followed by an additional equivalent capacity the following year in 2029, bringing the total to 2.4GW. GS expects that, based on IT load, this data center will rank first in Asia and between 10th and 15th globally. Facilities ranking higher are predominantly located in the United States. The employment impact is also substantial. According to GS, approximately 70,000 jobs will be created during the construction period, and direct employment alone is estimated to reach 2,000 after completion. Additional benefits are also anticipated, including increased floating population, revitalization of the service sector, and enhanced city brand value. Lee Ju-heon, head of Gangwon State's AI Data Center Promotion Team, explained at the signing ceremony, "President Lee Jae-myung presented a national growth governance blueprint for South Korea to leap into the world's top three AI powers and top five global powers, and in June announced the three major mega projects for South Korea's great leap forward, centered on semiconductors, physical AI, and the construction of AI data centers as core infrastructure." He added, "In line with this national policy direction, GS Group has now begun pursuing the Donghae AI Data Center project in earnest, strategically linked with global IT companies and based on the abundant power infrastructure of the east coast region, including renewable energy, and stable site conditions." GS Vice Chairman Hong Soon-ki emphasized, "GS Group selected AI data centers as a future business for the group and has been diligently preparing. Speed is critical. If we succeed in this project with speed, it will have significant ripple effects on regional economic revitalization, job creation, and the development of related ecosystems, and will serve as an important catalyst for changing South Korea's future industrial landscape." Governor Woo Sang-ho reflected, "Catching two birds with one stone — industrial transformation and regional cooperative development — has long been President Lee Jae-myung's strategy, and this year, this great opportunity has begun to bear fruit in reality." He continued, "I once again pledge that the provincial and municipal governments will cooperate to the fullest extent on administrative support, including permitting and approvals, to ensure GS's investment plan grows smoothly and that the largest AI center in Asia succeeds." In particular, Governor Woo repeatedly promised swift administrative support, stating, "We will meticulously prepare a support strategy and assist GS Group at a 'surprisingly fast speed.'" Donghae Mayor Lee Jeong-hak stated, "The AI data center campus is a core project that will enhance Donghae City's future industrial competitiveness. We will closely cooperate with relevant agencies and actively support the smooth progress of the project." Commitment to power infrastructure support was also confirmed. KEPCO Gangwon Headquarters Chief Lee Cheol-hyu said, "It was regrettable that Gangwon State, despite possessing tremendous energy resources such as renewable energy, solar power, and wind power, had to send surplus electricity to the Seoul metropolitan area and South Korea's Chungcheong region because its industry could not expand. Now that Gangwon State faces a great opportunity with large-scale investments from major corporations, I will provide maximum support as the head of KEPCO's Gangwon headquarters." Meanwhile, with this agreement as a catalyst, voices are emerging that SK Group's AI center project in the Gangneung area — which has been struggling with precise site selection due to power supply issues — should also have its details finalized promptly through KEPCO's broad-minded decision-making. As large-scale AI infrastructure investments continue in Gangwon State, attention is focused on whether South Korea's east coast region will emerge as a core hub for the nation's AI industry. title: Valkyries 88-83 Dream (Jul 4, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: ATLANTA -- — Veronica Burton scored 21 points and Gabby Williams had 14 of her 19 points in the second half to help the Golden State Valkyries complete a season sweep of the Atlanta Dream with an 88-83 victory on Saturday. Burton made 6 of 9 shots, with two 3-pointers and 7 of 8 free throws for Golden State (14-7) in its fourth straight victory. Williams sank 7 of 14 shots, including four 3-pointers, to help the Valkyries hand Atlanta (12-9) its fifth straight loss. Reserve Janelle Salaun had three 3s and scored 14 points. Allisha Gray led the Dream with 22 points and Angel Reese had 17 points and 13 rebounds for her 14th double-double of the season. Rhyne Howard hit four 3-pointers and scored 19 points, while reserve Madina Okot added 11. Reese scored five straight points to give Atlanta a 77-74 lead with 3:16 remaining. Williams had with a three-point play, Burton hit a go-ahead jumper and Kaila Charles buried a 3-pointer in an 8-0 run and the Valkyries stayed in front over the final 1:38. Golden State jumped out to a 12-2 lead that Atlanta quickly erased with an 11-0 run in a game that saw 22 lead changes and 14 ties. Golden State finished with a season-high 15 steals after handing Atlanta back-to-back losses to start the Dream's 0-4 road trip. Golden State: At Washington Mystics on Monday. Approximately 4,400 Georgia Southern University students will graduate with associate, baccalaureate, master’s, specialist and doctoral degrees for the 2026 Spring semester during four ceremonies in Statesboro and Savannah next week. According to a release from Georgia Southern, Candidates will have the option to choose the location where they would like to graduate. The dates, colleges and speakers for each ceremony are: ➤ Undergraduate ceremony for the College of Science and Mathematics, College of Arts and Humanities, Waters College of Health Professions, Jiann-Ping Hsu College of Public Health, Allen E. Paulson College of Engineering and Computing Bob Somers (’83) is the senior vice president of global sales at Delta Air Lines, where he is responsible for the company’s relationship with its largest corporate, agency and specialty accounts. Joining Delta in 1983, Somers also served as managing director of corporate and specialty sales and general manager of global corporate sales, following earlier roles in airport customer service and marketing, advertising and sales promotions. He is a member of the Global Business Travel Association (GBTA), and in 2016 was honored as the GBTA Allied Member of the Year and Business Travel News’ 25 Most Influential Business Travel Executives. Former chairman of the Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl, Somers currently serves on the boards for Foundation for Hospital Art, Bobby Dodd Coach of the Year, Atlanta Convention & Visitors Bureau and the Atlanta Sports Council. Somers earned a bachelor’s in public relations from Georgia Southern University. ▲ 6 p.m. — The Jack and Ruth Ann Hill Convocation Center in Statesboro ➤ Graduate ceremony for students in all colleges on any campus Nick Westbrook (’20), is the owner and operator of Chick-fil-A Hinesville and has built one of the top-performing locations in Georgia, earning multiple national excellence awards. A dedicated community leader who is passionate about leadership, mentorship and creating a hospitality culture, Westbrook has awarded more than $175,000 in scholarships through the Chick-fil-A Remarkable Futures Scholarship program. Westbrook earned an MBA from the Parker College of Business at Georgia Southern University. ➤ Undergraduate ceremony for students in all colleges on any campus Berry Aldridge (’15) is director of recruiting for the Banana Ball Championship League’s six teams. Prior to this role, he served in various capacities for The Savannah Bananas from 2016 to 2020, including director of tickets and vice president. In 2021, Aldridge shifted his focus to help create and launch the new sport of Banana Ball. Additionally in 2021, Aldridge became a licensed real estate agent and has since helped buyers and sellers across the Coastal Empire. Aldridge earned a bachelor’s in English literature from Armstrong State University. ➤ Undergraduate ceremony for students in the College of Education, Parker College of Business and College of Behavioral and Social Sciences Double Eagle Kim Hartsock (’20, ’21) is a certified public accountant. Appointed as the inaugural chair of the Parker College of Business Young Alumni Board, she also serves on the board of directors for the Georgia Southern University Foundation and the Parker College of Business. In addition, Hartsock is the board chair of the Gwinnett Chamber of Commerce, vice chair of the Community Foundation for Northeast Georgia and a board member for Leadership Gwinnett. Recognized as a two-time Titan 100 Georgia award winner, Hartsock was named by the Atlanta Business Chronicle in 2022 as “Most Admired CEO” and included in the 2014 Atlanta Business Chronicle’s “40 Under 40” Class. Hartsock earned a BBA in accounting and a master’s in accounting from Georgia Southern University.

title: "Full of Dr-gs, Full of Cr-p": Urban Meyer Doesn't Hold Back on Brutal Reality of Former Program - Yahoo Sports
content: Urban Meyer still remembers the trip to Missouri in his first year at Bowling Green in 2001. The setting didn’t mirror a program that had won only one game the year before. More than 70,000 fans filled the stadium. Missouri had the size, the depth, and the reputation. Bowling Green arrived with barely enough healthy bodies and almost no expectations from the outside world. Yet Meyer told his players not to chase the scoreboard. The goal was smaller. Get first downs. Gain four yards. Make tackles. Repeat it again and again until the game changes shape. By the fourth quarter, Bowling Green was one drive away from an upset victory. And they finally won it, 20-13. That night became the first public sign that Meyer believed culture could beat talent gaps. Even when the team had deep-seated problems and a hopeless culture. “When I went to Bowling Green, they were one and 10, two and nine. Just a dismal place. And a lot of kids got kicked out,” Meyer said on the Breaking Sales Podcast on June 15. “They really didn’t get kicked off; they just quit. And they should have quit. It was a team that was full of dr-gs and full of cr-p, and it was kind of a joke to be honest with you. But the ones who stayed were the most resilient, the greatest kids I have ever been around.” At 36, Meyer had never been a head coach; his résumé was assistant roles at Notre Dame, Colorado State, and Utah, where he built a reputation as a creative receivers coach and offensive mind. Bowling Green became his first chance to run an entire program. The pressure was immediate. He later said players were leaving the program instead of fighting through hard times. Some quit. Others disappeared from the roster for disciplinary reasons. He remembered the roster shrinking from around 100 players to nearly 60 or 65 by the time the season started. His first rule was simple: go to class. Show up on time. Finish workouts. Compete every day. Players who would not buy in were not carried along. The roster got smaller, but Meyer believed the players who stayed became tougher because of it. That philosophy followed Meyer everywhere. At Bowling Green, then at Utah, Florida, and Ohio State, Meyer pushed a formula built on accountability and repetition. His famous formula, E + R = O, has guided him everywhere. That loosely translates to Event plus Response equals Outcome. Players can’t control everything that happens to them. However, they can control how they react. So, practices became intense. Details mattered, and relentless effort became non-negotiable. The Missouri game perfectly mirrored that philosophy. “The team won one game the year before, and that’s all we did was get first downs,” Meyer said about the Missouri game. “We got first down, first down, first down, first down. On defense, we kept tackling. And sure enough, we’re there, 5 minutes left in the fourth quarter. We need to score a touchdown. And we do.” Bowling Green finished 8-3 in Meyer’s first season. The Falcons then went 9-3 in the second year.
